summary: This standards-track document extends the IANA IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry. The registry says which TLVs may appear in which PDUs but not which can appear in purges. This adds a record of permitted TLVs in purges and updates a related earlier specification.

plainLanguage.summary: There is an official list of which labels may go in which messages, and it missed one kind of message. This adds a column for that kind.

questions: which tlvs are allowed in is-is purge
which tlvs allowed in is-is purge
subtitle: Registry rules for what metadata can appear in link state purge messages.

tldr.problem: IS-IS uses purges to discard old link state information, but the IANA registry did not document which metadata items (TLVs) could appear in purges, creating ambiguity.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6233 extends the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry with a purge column showing which TLVs are allowed in purges, and clarifies authentication handling for purges.
tldr.outcome: The registry now provides a definitive list of allowed TLVs in purges, helping implementers and aiding future protocol extensions.

today: RFC 6233 is a Proposed Standard that clarified the IS-IS purge registry and remains in use as the definitive reference for which TLVs are allowed in purges.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IS-IS routing protocol, defined in ISO 10589, maintains a link state database by flooding Link State Protocol Data Units (LSPs). When an LSP is no longer needed, IS-IS uses a purge mechanism: the originating router sets the Remaining Lifetime to zero and floods the purged LSP so other routers discard the old information.

Historically, purges retained only the LSP header and removed all TLVs (Type-Length-Value metadata fields). Later enhancements like RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 (authentication) required certain TLVs to appear in purges. However, the IANA IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry did not document which TLVs are permissible in purges. RFC 6233 remedies this gap and updates the authentication rules.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router stops using old route information, it sends a message saying 'forget this' with a lifetime of zero. The rules for what can go in that message were unclear and needed fixing.

sections.title: Registry Extension
sections.content:
RFC 6233 adds a Purge column to the existing IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry. Each TLV row now has a purge status: 'y' means the TLV may appear in purges; 'n' means it must not. Initially, only two TLV types have 'y' status: type 10 (Authentication) and type 137 (Dynamic hostname). All other TLVs default to 'n'.

The purge status applies to all sub-TLVs nested within a TLV. This single registry serves as the definitive list of allowed TLVs in purges, aiding both implementers and future protocol designers.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry now has a column saying 'OK to put in purge message' or 'not OK'. Only authentication and hostname labels are allowed by default.

sections.title: Purges and Authentication
sections.content:
RFC 6233 updates the authentication rules from RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. Implementations that support authentication must reject any purge containing a TLV not listed in the registry as purge-safe. A purge may contain an unknown TLV only if it also carries the Purge Originator Identification (POI) TLV from RFC 6232.

When generating a purge, an authenticating router first removes all non-purge TLVs, adds the POI TLV, optionally adds other allowed TLVs, and finally computes authentication over the result. If a router receives a purge without POI and adds the POI itself, it must recompute authentication. Purges received with the correct TLVs and authentication must be forwarded without modification.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router protects messages with authentication, it checks that incoming purges have only the labels they're allowed to have. When sending a purge, it builds it with the right labels and signs it.
